# Letter Auction Playbook

When I see the letter values and lexicon at the start, I will immediately identify the highest-value words I can potentially spell and which letters are essential to them.

When bidding on early letters, I will recognize that low-value letters (A, E, S, T, R at 1 point each) will likely go unsold if I bid conservatively, so I should not waste coins on them. I will bid 0 on most 1-point letters unless I have a specific word strategy that requires them.

When I've won a few letters, I will check if I can already spell any word from the lexicon with what I own, and bias my remaining bids toward completing high-scoring words rather than collecting random letters.

When a letter gets a tie bid and goes unsold, I will recognize this as a signal that my opponent is also being cautious, so I can continue bidding low on subsequent low-value letters.

When I have a high-value letter like M (3 points) but no supporting letters yet, I will be more aggressive in bidding on subsequent letters that enable words using M. One letter alone cannot form any word, so I need to pair it with common letters early before my opponent locks them down.

When I see my opponent winning multiple letters in sequence (like T, S, T, A), I will recognize they are building toward a completable word and adjust my strategy to either outbid them on critical letters or accept that I need to build a different word path.

When submitting my word, I will only claim words that I can actually spell with the letters I own. I will not assume letters I don't have are available.

When I cannot spell any word from the lexicon with my current letters, I will submit [word: none] and rely on my unspent coins for points rather than waste time trying to invent words.

I will treat unspent coins as a failure of execution. If I end with many coins and no word, it means I bid too passively early and should have fought harder for letters that would let me form even a 2-3 letter word.

My goal should be to spend coins on letters that form words, not to preserve coins. A word scored is always better than unspent coins if the word is worth more than the coins' point value.

# Letter Auction Playbook

When I see the auction start, I recognize that I need to actively win letters to score points. Sitting out and waiting for cheap opportunities guarantees I end with nothing.

When a letter comes up for auction, I bid aggressively enough to actually win it. My bids of 4, 3, 2, 0, 0, 0, 3, 2 in the last game won me exactly the letters I needed (R, S, T, A, E) and formed a valid word, but I scored 0 because I spent all 12 coins and had no unspent coins to add to my word score.

When evaluating a letter's worth, I consider both its point value and whether winning it gives me a chance to form a high-scoring word. A single letter is useless; I need a collection. But I must also consider the cost: overpaying leaves me with few unspent coins at the end.

When I bid conservatively to "preserve coins," I must recognize the balance: I need enough coins left over at the end to contribute meaningfully to my final score. Unspent coins are worth 1 point each.

When the opponent shows spending patterns (bidding aggressively early), I should match or outbid them on letters I truly need, but I should also recognize when I'm in a bidding war and pull back to conserve coins for the endgame.

When common vowels like E and A come up for auction, I bid to win them at a reasonable price. Vowels are essential to word formation but I should not overpay for them.

When I see letters go unsold at 0/0 bids, I recognize this as an opportunity I should have exploited—I should have won them with minimal coins spent, freeing up my budget for more strategic purchases.

When the auction is halfway through and I have won 2-3 useful letters, I should evaluate whether I can form a word from what I have and whether the remaining letters are worth pursuing or whether I should focus on preserving coins.

When I have the letters needed to form a word (especially a vowel-consonant mix that makes 4-5 letters), I should consider bidding 0 on subsequent letters and letting my opponent overpay, so I retain coins for the final score.

When I finish the auction, my final score is: (2 × sum of letter values in my word) + unspent coins. Both components matter equally. A word worth 5 points plus 2 unspent coins gives 7 total; a word worth 5 points plus 0 unspent coins gives 5 total.

When I spend coins, I should aim to spend roughly 8-9 of my 12 coins across the auction, winning 4-5 high-utility letters, leaving 3-4 coins unspent for the final score.

My next game: I will bid to win letters actively in the first 4-5 rounds, prioritizing vowels (A, E) and common consonants (R, S, T, M) at reasonable prices (1-3 coins each). Once I have 4-5 letters that form a word, I will bid 0 on remaining letters to preserve coins. I will end with unspent coins and a valid word.
